Title: The distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with tool transfers to minimize the total tardiness
Authors: Martin Schönheit, Tristan Becker, Rainer Lasch
Abstract: Competitive pressure and economic growth have driven firms to diversify their production locations to access customer and raw material markets. The resulting production networks require coordinated planning across multiple factories, leading to distributed scheduling problems. In industrial production networks, processing at certain machines requires specialized and costly tools that are only available at a subset of factories, thereby inducing factory-eligibility constraints. Despite their practical relevance, such constraints have been largely overlooked in the scheduling literature over the past 15 years. We address this gap by extending the distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem to incorporate eligibility constraints arising from tool availability, evolving dynamically through tool transfers between factories. To support on-time delivery while accounting for geographically dispersed factories, the model incorporates factory-dependent due dates and minimizes total tardiness. Accordingly, we develop three solution approaches: a novel network-flow-based mixed-integer programming model, a constraint programming formulation, and a tailored Iterated Greedy algorithm that reduces total tardiness by an average of 7.7% compared to the constraint programming approach for large instances. Computational experiments further show that tool transfers reduce total tardiness by 21.67% on average compared with static tool allocation. A sensitivity analysis confirms that tool transfers remain beneficial across varying tool redundancy levels and geographic network configurations.

Title: A multi-period vehicle routing problem with driver consistency and arrival-time diversification
Authors: Jahir Llagas, Foteini Stavropoulou, Sanne Wøhlk
Abstract: We study a Multi-Period Vehicle Routing Problem that integrates driver consistency and arrival-time diversification. Driver consistency requires each customer to be served by the same vehicle across all service periods, while arrival-time diversification enforces temporal separation between visits in different periods. We first propose a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming formulation and an exact Logic-Based Benders Decomposition implemented through a Branch-and-Check scheme, where a multi-period VRP with driver consistency is handled in the master problem and arrival-time diversification is addressed in the subproblem. Building on this structure, we develop a matheuristic that exploits the subproblem in an efficient and targeted manner. As arrival-time diversification checks are computationally expensive, we propose a feasibility check procedure over a restricted search space. Computational results show that the branch-and-check approach solves medium-scale instances to optimality, while the matheuristic achieves near-optimal solutions in significantly shorter computation times. Lastly, the impact of arrival-time diversification is examined and managerial insights are derived.

Title: Scheduling electricity production units to mitigate severe weather impact: An efficient computational implementation
Authors: Yongzheng Dai, Antonio J. Conejo, Feng Qiu
Abstract: Extreme weather events in electric power systems can cause line trips or physical damage to transmission infrastructure, potentially leading to large-scale load shedding. To mitigate this risk, we propose a framework that strategically pre-positions the commitment of generation units--particularly slow-start units--to adapt to transmission topologies that may arise following such events. The objective is to minimize load shedding under worst-case conditions. This paper makes two main contributions. First, we provide a more accurate representation of the underlying physical laws than those used in prior studies. Second, we develop a highly efficient solution algorithm that outperforms state-of-the-art, off-the-shelf solvers. The proposed framework is formulated as a two-stage robust optimization model. In the first stage, generation units are scheduled in anticipation of disruptions. In the second stage, power dispatch decisions are optimized to minimize load shedding under the worst-case transmission topology. To ensure system reliability and security, we incorporate convexified AC power flow constraints. The resulting model is a tri-level mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem. To address its computational complexity, we design a problem-specific outer approximation algorithm embedded within a column-and-constraint generation framework. Computational results show that the proposed model and solution approach can achieve solutions within a standard optimality gap in a reasonable time for moderately large instances.

Title: New solutions for the multi-skilled resource-constrained project scheduling problem with a satisfiability solver
Authors: Mario Vanhoucke, José Coelho
Abstract: This paper presents a SAT-based algorithm for solving the multi-skilled resource-constrained project scheduling problem (MSRCPSP). The proposed approach translates the problem’s precedence, resource and skill constraints into a Boolean satisfiability formulation, enabling both lower- and upper-bound strategies to efficiently explore the solution space. Comprehensive computational experiments are conducted on four benchmark datasets, comparing fast heuristics, consisting of 18 lower bounds, several priority-rule-based upper bounds and a simulated annealing algorithm, with three intensive optimization procedures consisting of a CPLEX model and a genetic algorithm from the literature and the proposed SAT procedure of the current study. The results show that the SAT-based algorithm is particularly effective in improving lower bounds and can also refine upper bounds. When combined with other optimization methods, it significantly tightens both bounds for a large portion of instances. Despite these improvements, a number of challenging open instances remain, suggesting opportunities for further research. All data and updated solutions, including both lower and upper bounds for the four datasets, are publicly available.

Title: Group compromise rankings with indirect preference information: Maximizing pairwise- and rank-based support
Authors: Zhuolin Li, Zhen Zhang, Miłosz Kadziński
Abstract: In recent years, deriving compromise rankings that reconcile the diverse opinions of Decision Makers (DMs) has become a central theme in group decision making. Yet, most existing methods assume that DMs can directly specify the parameters required by the underlying model (e.g., criteria weights or marginal value functions), which may impose a considerable cognitive burden. To address this, we develop novel methods for constructing compromise rankings from a preference disaggregation perspective, relying solely on indirect preference information provided by DMs. Two complementary variants are considered: one based on pairwise preference relations and the other on rank assignments. In both cases, individual support degrees are first defined – either for preference/indifference relations among alternatives or for assigning alternatives to specific rank positions. Optimization models are then formulated to aggregate these individual measures into group support degrees. Finally, subsequent models maximize group support across all pairs or all rank assignments, thereby producing the group compromise ranking. The proposed methodology is illustrated with a project proposal ranking problem from the literature, followed by robustness analyses. Computational experiments under varying parameter settings further benchmark the methods against existing approaches, confirming their effectiveness. A comparative discussion further clarifies the methodological and practical advantages of the proposed approaches.

Title: Leveraging hypercube queueing approximations in joint coverage models for the military medical evacuation location–allocation problem with multiple distinct servers

Title: Service network design with uncertainty on water levels for intermodal river transport
Authors: Bita Payami, Ioana C. Bilegan, Teodor Gabriel Crainic, Walter Rei
Abstract: . Barge transport presents a sustainable alternative to road transport, offering the potential to alleviate congestion and reduce costs. However, increasingly frequent and severe drought seasons, attributed to climate change, challenge the resilience of this mode of transport. Decreased water levels restrict navigation, impact vessel size, and reduce vessel capacity. This study introduces a novel and integrated modeling framework for tactical planning in consolidation-based barge freight transportation. By examining the relationship between water levels and vessel load capacity, with a specific focus on vessel dimensions, the framework aims to evaluate possible impacts on the efficiency and profitability of inland waterway transport. We also introduce two stochastic Water-Level-Constrained Scheduled Service Network Design with Resource and Revenue Management models to address uncertainties in resource capacities caused by water level variations, each addressing a distinct tactical plan adjustment strategy. These models aim to establish a tactical plan, given predicted water levels, that maximizes the expected carrier’s revenue while accounting for future adjustments to the plan when information is revealed and predictions are reliably updated, to fulfill the demands of shippers and optimize the utilization of the carrier’s resources. Through extensive experimentation using commercial software and a novel decision-based scenario clustering algorithm, we assess the quality of the solutions obtained with the different model variants and analyze the impact of the water level on the results.

Title: Going the extra mile — By design: Generating road networks with target values of travel impedance via bi-level optimization
Authors: Steven Parks, Selene Silvestri, Matthias Winkenbach
Abstract: The inherent characteristics of a road network impact transportation system design, performance, and user behavior. However, systematically evaluating their impacts on vehicle routing, facility location, and other transportation decisions is challenging. In this work, we propose a methodology to generate stylized road networks that satisfy user-defined values of average network circuity and inefficiency, two graph characteristics that, respectively, describe the closeness of spatial locations in terms of shortest travel distance and time. We refine an exact solution approach consisting of two novel bi-level mixed-integer Road Network Design Problems solved in succession. We concoct a suite of test instances to evaluate their computational performance and demonstrate that our proposed linearizations, valid inequalities, and warm start heuristics significantly improve model tractability. The resulting method enables the generation of road networks with prescribed values of average travel impedance. As such, it lays a groundwork for future research on the impacts of road network structure and connectivity on transportation systems.

Title: Self-adaptive interval strategies for exact line search: Application to traffic assignment problems
Authors: Zhengyang Li, Anthony Chen
Abstract: Step size determination in optimization is often performed via line search. Interval reduction methods, such as golden-section and bisection, are widely used for exact line search but require multiple function and/or derivative evaluations at each outer iteration of the optimization algorithm (e.g., Frank–Wolfe). In this paper, we propose two simple yet effective self-adaptive interval strategies, one based on zero-order information and the other on first-order information, that adaptively determine the search interval at each iteration using step size information from the previous iteration. We integrate these strategies into the exact line search procedure commonly used in the Frank–Wolfe algorithm and apply them to three traffic assignment problems with different complexities: classical user equilibrium (UE), bi-criteria user equilibrium (BUE), and multiclass bi-criteria user equilibrium (MBUE). Numerical results demonstrate that the self-adaptive interval strategies considerably accelerate classical exact line search methods, reducing the number of function and/or derivative evaluations by up to 52%. This translates into considerable CPU time reductions when function and derivative evaluations are computationally expensive.

Title: Dynamic idle-time bounding mechanism for job shop scheduling problems
Authors: Christian Perez, Rubén Mas, Miguel A. Salido
Abstract: The Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (JSP) is a well-known NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with broad relevance to industrial scheduling applications. Given its inherent computational complexity, effective filtering and bounding strategies are essential for reducing search effort. This study proposes a dynamic idle-time bounding mechanism that restricts the search to statistically plausible idle-time intervals before and during the solution process. Idle-time thresholds, conditioned on instance size, are estimated via polynomial regression on empirical solver performance data and adaptively relaxed when necessary to preserve feasibility. The resulting mechanism prunes unpromising regions of the search space and strengthens propagation within conventional exact solvers. The mechanism is implemented as a solver-agnostic augmentation for exact solvers and evaluated on Taillard’s benchmark set and JSPLIB instances using CPLEX, Gurobi, and OR-Tools. The results show substantial reductions in solving time, reaching up to 80% on several benchmark families, while maintaining competitive returned-solution quality under common time budgets; in multiple hard instances, the optimality gap is also reduced. Overall, the proposed method is particularly effective on medium and large JSP instances, where idle-time decisions introduce substantial combinatorial degeneracy, and provides a practical enhancement for scalable exact scheduling.

Title: Multi-product batch scheduling for cement mills under time-of-use electricity tariffs
Authors: Liteng An, Songlin Zhang, Xiaochen Hao
Abstract: As a high energy-consuming facility in the cement industry, cement mills require effective production scheduling strategies to reduce electricity costs under time-of-use (TOU) pricing while satisfying the demand for multiple cement products. This study develops an optimization model for cement mill scheduling based on a mixed-integer programming (MIP) approach, with the objective of reducing electricity costs while satisfying the demand for multiple types of cement. The model first ensures that the production targets for each cement type are satisfied. Subsequently, it optimizes the scheduling of production batches and the allocation of equipment to facilitate load shifting towards periods of lower electricity tariffs, thereby minimizing total electricity costs and enhancing both the economic efficiency and practical applicability of the scheduling strategy. Furthermore, the model explicitly incorporates sequence-dependent setup times and energy consumption during machine startup and shutdown processes, realistically capturing the impact of product switching and intermittent production on overall scheduling performance, thereby improving the operational and engineering applicability of the model. In terms of solution methodology, an Improved Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization (IDPSO) algorithm based on greedy insertion decoding is proposed to generate feasible production schedules. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, a set of computational experiments was designed. Simulation studies based on real-world data from a cement plant demonstrate that the model not only ensures timely fulfillment of cement demand but also effectively avoids production during high-tariff periods and reduces cost impacts associated with machine startup, shutdown, and setup times.

Title: Reinforcement learning-driven non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II for in-space manufacturing energy efficient scheduling problem with power constraint
Authors: Liping Xu, Kai Li, Chuanyu Wu, Han Zhang
Abstract: As deep space exploration missions continue to expand and the operational costs of space stations rise, there is a growing need to focus on in-space manufacturing production and energy management. Addressing the complex characteristics of energy constraints, equipment multi-functionality, and multi-constrained production in space manufacturing, this paper investigates a flexible job-shop energy-efficient scheduling problem that considers power threshold and variable processing speeds, aiming to balance production efficiency and energy consumption. Firstly, a bi-objective optimization mathematical model incorporating power constraint, variable processing speeds, setup and transportation constraints is constructed. Secondly, a reinforcement learning-driven non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (RLNSGA-II) is proposed. This algorithm employs a hybrid population initialization method, combining various scheduling rules to generate the initial population. An adaptive local search strategy is designed to choose appropriate operators for individuals. Meanwhile, a Q-learning-driven strategy is applied to determine the local search depth during the evolutionary process, aiming to enhance optimization performance without increasing computational time. Finally, the performance of RLNSGA-II is evaluated using 45 test instances. Ablation experiments demonstrate that each component contributes to enhancing overall performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of these innovative designs. Furthermore, compared with other intelligent algorithms, RLNSGA-II performs better on the Hypervolume and Inverted Generational Distance metrics in 80% and 75.6% of instances, respectively, thus validating its effectiveness.

Title: The lecture-hall quadratic assignment problem
Authors: Tal Raviv
Abstract: We study the post-timetabling lecture-hall assignment problem : given a fixed weekly timetable and realized student enrollments, assign each lecture to a compatible hall so as to minimize the walking burden of students moving between consecutive lectures, plus a penalty for feasible but non-ideal hall–lecture assignments. The problem combines a quadratic assignment objective, driven by shared enrollments and hall-to-hall distances, with interval-scheduling feasibility and hall-capacity constraints. We prove that it is NP-hard and, unless P = N P , inapproximable within any fixed rational factor, already in a single-day, two-block special case. We develop two exact mathematical-programming formulations: a bilinear mixed-integer quadratic program and a compact mixed-integer linear program with one distance variable per successor pair. To tighten the models we introduce biclique distance cuts that dominate the standard pairwise linking inequalities, complemented by Chvátal-Gomory capacity-dominance cuts; common side constraints such as SameRoom and SameAttendees are accommodated as well. In experiments on 35 daily instances derived from five large ITC 2019 competition benchmarks and a 2023 institutional dataset from Lancaster University, the biclique-strengthened compact linearized program solves every instance to proven optimality within an 1800-second limit. The direct quadratic model often finds the same incumbents but is weaker for proving optimality on the hardest instances, while the biclique cuts are the dominant modeling device behind the observed speed and robustness. On the ten Lancaster instances, optimized assignments reduce model-implied walking by 20%–45% relative to the deployed room plan.

Title: A pipeline methodology for neural network accelerators under a throughput constraint
Authors: Ali Oudrhiri, Alix Munier Kordon
Abstract: Neural networks have gained widespread popularity, particularly in the context of hardware accelerators. These accelerators are typically designed according to optimization criteria such as throughput, power consumption, and energy efficiency, which involve inherent trade-offs. They generally consist of a neural processing unit with a configurable number of parallel processing elements, along with internal memory resources. This paper investigates the feasibility of improving processing throughput and achieving better trade-offs by introducing an additional optimization dimension. Specifically, we explore a pipelined configuration involving multiple distinct instances of the neural processing unit.We propose a simple and generic methodology applicable to a wide range of feed-forward neural network accelerators. We show that the problem can be formulated as a specific case of the assembly line balancing problem, and we extend a well-known dynamic programming approach with polynomial time complexity to solve it exactly. The proposed methodology is validated on a real-world industrial hardware accelerator prototype, for which evaluation functions for the relevant criteria are available. Experimental results demonstrate that the pipelined configuration significantly increases system throughput without degrading the other considered criteria.

Title: Evaluating sensitivity of distributionally robust optimization models
Authors: Yi Zhao, Jun Li, Shuming Wang
Abstract: This paper develops a sensitivity computation framework for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) models with event-wise ambiguity set, quantifying how the worst-case loss responds to perturbations of the ambiguity-set parameters, including mean bounds, dispersion radii, and scenario probabilities. This framework covers many commonly-used loss functions and dispersion measures and therefore accommodates extensive well-studied DRO applications in the operations management community such as portfolio optimization and chance-constrained program. We first exploit the decomposable structure of the event-wise ambiguity set and derive a scenario-wise dual reformulation of the worst-case loss. We then establish the compactness of the optimal dual solution set for two common loss functions. Leveraging this dual reformulation together with the compactness of the optimal dual set, we next derive directional derivative of the worst-case loss and derive its computationally tractable formula, obtained by solving a small convex optimization subproblem. To achieve meaningful comparisons across heterogeneous parameters, we introduce scenario-wise and globally averaged normalized sensitivity indices that convert the directional derivatives into dimensionless, elasticity-like measures. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous first-order expansion of the worst-case loss under arbitrary parameter perturbations. Finally, we validate the practical efficacy of our framework through extensive numerical experiments on a redundancy allocation problem, demonstrating how the sensitivity map identifies critical ambiguity-set parameters, and how the choice of dispersion measure affects robustness to data outliers.

Title: Task assignment and multi-AGV collision-free path planning considering integrated picking and replenishment in robotic mobile fulfillment systems
Authors: Xuefang Han, Kunpeng Li, P.N. Ram Kumar
Abstract: Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) are essential to the logistics frameworks within contemporary e-commerce warehouses. These systems involve three primary aspects of decision-making: rack-to-AGV assignment, AGV path planning, and conflict mediation for multiple AGVs. While substantial research has been dedicated to these elements in isolation, comprehensive integrated studies addressing the problem holistically are still relatively few. This study introduces a co-optimization problem for task assignment and global path planning for multiple AGVs in RMFS, effectively integrating dispatching, conflict-free routing, and scheduling of these vehicles. We formulate this problem as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model, aimed at minimizing the total operational time of AGVs and the maximum picking completion time. Given that the problem is NP-hard, efficiently solving the MILP model for realistic-scale instances presents significant challenges. To address this issue, we developed a two-echelon K-Means and an enhanced conflict-based search algorithm. This approach allocates racks to AGVs using the K-Means algorithm while planning conflict-free paths for AGVs through an enhanced conflict-based search method. Furthermore, we rigorously analyze key structural properties of the problem, revealing several theoretically grounded properties embedded within the algorithm’s logic. To ensure high-quality lower bounds, we propose a relaxation model that does not involve planning paths for AGVs. Our experimental results indicate that: (i) our algorithm achieves solutions with minimal optimality gaps compared to the high-quality lower bounds developed; (ii) it outperforms existing benchmark algorithms in terms of solution quality and demonstrates superior computational efficiency; and (iii) the proposed properties significantly enhance the algorithm’s performance. In conclusion, this paper presents a robust and tailored approach to RMFS, providing valuable managerial insights to empower warehouse operators in their decision-making processes.

Title: Advanced probabilistic tabu search for the fair max-min diversity problem
Authors: He Zheng, Anna Martínez-Gavara, Rafael Martí, Fred Glover
Abstract: The concept of fairness in optimization models has opened up a wide range of practical applications, ranging from the equitable access to services in location, to team formation problems in human resources. Recently, the concept of fairness has found applications in the important area of maximizing diversity, giving rise to the Fair Max-Min Diversity (FMMD) problem which incorporates group fairness constraints. In this paper, we target this novel variant of the well-known Max-Min Diversity Problem (MMDP) that constitutes a challenge for today’s solvers. We explore two metaheuristic paradigms to develop new solution methods for the FMMD problem: Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP) and Probabilistic Tabu Search (PTS). A computational study reveals that incorporating memory mechanisms makes PTS particularly effective in solving FMMD instances. To further enhance performance, we propose an advanced version of PTS that integrates memory-based perturbation and strategic oscillation mechanisms. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate that our advanced PTS consistently outperforms basic metaheuristics on all problems and achieves significantly superior performance relative to the exact approaches for larger problems. Additional analysis highlights the contributions of each proposed component, offering insights into the design of efficient methods for diversity optimization under fairness constraints.

Title: Small and large neighborhood search for the on-demand bus routing problem: A bus stop assignment and transportation problem
Authors: Jorge Mortes, Martin Cousineau, Fabien Lehuédé, Jorge E. Mendoza, María I. Restrepo
Abstract: This article investigates a static on-demand transportation problem in which users are picked up and dropped off at existing bus stops. Specifically, the selection of bus stops for each request, along with the bus routes, is simultaneously determined by the booking system using an optimization algorithm. We focus on service quality by lexicographically minimizing request travel time (including both walking time and time spent on the bus) and total route length. We introduce a matheuristic algorithm based on small and large neighborhood search, incorporating state-of-the-art operators and a set covering component. The algorithm is tested on a new set of instances, based on real data from New York City, which we propose as a future benchmark. On our New York City instances, this algorithm outperforms prior approaches by finding feasible solutions for all instances and reducing user ride time by more than 5%; it also performs well on related benchmark problems. Additionally, we discuss implementation details for decision-makers and practitioners.

Title: Behavior and representation in open-weight Large Language Models for combinatorial optimization: From feature extraction to algorithm selection
Authors: Francesca Da Ros, Luca Di Gaspero, Kevin Roitero
Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) open new perspectives for automation in optimization, yet little is known about whether their internal representations capture problem structure or algorithmic behavior. We investigate whether representations learned by frozen, open-weight LLMs for combinatorial optimization instances can support downstream decision tasks. The goal is not to replace exact feature extractors or to propose a new algorithm, but to assess whether such representations are reusable for feature recovery and algorithm selection. Our methodology combines direct querying , which tests explicit feature extraction, with probing analyses of whether this information is implicitly encoded in the hidden layers. The probing framework is further extended to a per-instance algorithm selection task. Experiments span four benchmark problems, three instance representations, and five open-weight models from 3B to 120B parameters across the Llama instruct and gpt-oss reasoning families, including a chain-of-thought study on Llama models. Results show a limited ability to recover features explicitly, particularly those requiring structured computation, while part of this information remains implicitly encoded in the hidden states. A consistent gap separates implicit encoding from explicit retrieval. Model scale attenuates this gap, whereas the effect of chain-of-thought prompting depends strongly on model size, and in all cases the gap remains open. Reasoning-oriented models also tend to abstain more when reliable computation is not possible. Notably, the predictive power of LLM hidden-layer representations is comparable to traditional feature extraction across all five models, indicating they can act as effective surrogate descriptors for downstream optimization tasks.

Title: An exact pruned route-enumeration and set-partitioning approach for the multi-pickup and delivery problem with time windows
Authors: Conor Kikkert, Michael Forbes
Abstract: The multi-pickup and delivery problem with time windows (MPDPTW) arises in on-demand logistics applications where each delivery corresponds to one or more pickups, all of which must be completed before the delivery. Existing exact methods for the MPDPTW typically rely on large mixed-integer programming formulations with extensive branching and cutting. This paper proposes PRE-SP, an exact pruned route-enumeration and set-partitioning framework that evaluates candidate single-vehicle request subsets a priori , discards infeasible subsets using pruning rules that preserve exactness, and then solves a set-partitioning master problem over the resulting feasible routes. Computational results on the 120 classical MPDPTW benchmark instances show that PRE-SP solves 116 instances to proven optimality within a 1-hour time limit, and all 120 when the time limit is extended to 24 hours for the remaining four cases, outperforming existing exact approaches on this benchmark set. Additional analysis of the explored search space shows how instance size, request length, and time-window structure affect the practical behaviour of the enumeration procedure. Experiments on 30 larger 200-node instances provide additional insight into the scalability limits of the framework. Overall, the results show that route enumeration with exactness-preserving pruning, combined with set partitioning, is a competitive exact solution framework for the MPDPTW on the benchmark classes studied.

Title: Coupling-aware destruction with large-language-model guidance for energy-efficient blocking hybrid flow shop scheduling
Authors: Shikun Chen
Abstract: The blocking hybrid flow shop with sequence-dependent setup times and time-of-use electricity pricing presents a bi-objective scheduling problem that requires simultaneous minimization of makespan and energy cost. Blocking constraints create hidden couplings between these two objectives, where a single constraint affects makespan and energy cost through different mechanisms, and the dominant coupling effect varies across regions of the Pareto front. Standard evolutionary baselines do not explicitly model this region-specific coupling structure. Our approach embeds a coupling-aware iterated greedy algorithm within a decomposition-based multi-objective framework, where a large language model (LLM) serves as a constraint-objective coupling analyzer. Rather than replace evolutionary operators, the LLM identifies which coupling dominates in each Pareto region and provides subproblem-specific destruction–construction strategies through a three-level phase-adaptive architecture. In the tested configuration, this design uses roughly thirty-one to forty-three LLM invocation opportunities per run. Computational experiments on adapted benchmark instances and steelmaking-continuous casting instances with real scheduling structure and representative energy parameters show that the proposed method attains higher hypervolume and lower inverted generational distance than nine comparison algorithms, including non-LLM variants with the same destruction-mode action space.

Title: A frequent pattern mining-based hybrid evolutionary algorithm for the k-clustering minimum biclique completion problem
Authors: Dawei Wu, Zhiying Zhang, Qing Zhou
Abstract: The k[jls-end-space/]-clustering minimum biclique completion problem (k[jls-end-space/]-CMBCP) is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem with important applications in areas such as multicast network design and supply chain management. Given a bipartite graph (Formula presented), the k[jls-end-space/]-CMBCP aims to partition U into k disjoint clusters Ui[jls-end-space/], and each cluster (Formula presented) contains all vertices in V that are adjacent to at least one vertex in Ui[jls-end-space/]. For each bipartite cluster (Formula presented), the induced subgraph is completed into a biclique by adding edges as needed. The objective is to minimize the total number of edges added across all clusters. This study proposes a frequent pattern mining-based hybrid evolutionary algorithm (FPMHEA) to effectively address the k[jls-end-space/]-CMBCP by exploiting structural information inherent in the problem graphs. The FPMHEA features a frequent pattern-based population initialization to generate high-quality and diverse initial solutions, a frequent pattern-guided crossover operator to strengthen search guidance during recombination, and an attribute-based tabu search with fast incremental evaluation for efficient local optimization. Extensive computational experiments on three widely used benchmark sets of 63 instances demonstrate that FPMHEA is highly competitive in both solution quality and computational efficiency compared with several state-of-the-art algorithms. Specifically, it improves the best-known upper bounds in literature for 44 instances and fails to match the best-known results on only 4 cases within short running times. Additional analysis further confirms the substantial contributions of the main algorithmic components to the overall performance of FPMHEA.

Title: A robust optimization approach for scheduling with uncertain start-time dependent costs
Authors: Sofía Rodríguez-Ballesteros, Javier Alcaraz, Laura Anton-Sanchez, Marc Goerigk, Dorothee Henke
Abstract: In this work, we study a single-machine scheduling problem that aims at minimizing the total cost of a schedule subject to start-time dependent costs. This framework naturally captures scenarios where costs fluctuate throughout the day, such as time-varying energy or labor prices. To model more realistic scenarios, we assume that these costs lie within a budgeted uncertainty set and propose a two-stage robust optimization approach. In a first stage, the order in which activities should be executed is decided. After a cost scenario has been revealed, the starting times for each activity are established, subject to the ordering from the first stage. We demonstrate that the proposed problem is NP-hard and not approximable, implying the complexity of its robust counterpart. Furthermore, we show that already evaluating a first-stage solution is NP-hard when the uncertainty set is discrete. We develop models and solution methods for both continuous and discrete budgeted uncertainty. In computational experiments, we compare these approaches and demonstrate the advantages of including uncertainty beforehand.

Title: End-to-end portfolio selection: Leveraging deep learning in Smart Predict then Optimize
Authors: Wenchu Zhang, Zhaolin Hu, Haiqing Yin
Abstract: The end-to-end prediction and optimization paradigm based on Smart “Predict, then Optimize” (SPO) method provides a new approach for portfolio selection. In this paper, we study the end-to-end portfolio selection by leveraging deep learning in the SPO framework. We consider several deep learning models including two linear models, two recurrent neural network models, and two transformer-based models for financial time series forecasting, and incorporate them in the SPO loss functions in the mean–variance models. We train the end-to-end models using the Adam algorithm based on the specific structure of the SPO+ function to directly obtain the optimal portfolio weights. We compare via the real test the end-to-end paradigm with the two-stage prediction and optimization paradigm that uses the conventional Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function, and illustrate the competitiveness of the former. Our tests also suggest that the iTransformer model appears to hold some superiority among the various deep learning models in this end-to-end portfolio selection practice.

Title: FastSC: A fast local search algorithm for the set covering problem
Authors: Jieyu Wu, Shiwei Pan, Yiyuan Wang, Minghao Yin
Abstract: The set covering problem (SCP) is one of the classical combinatorial optimization problems with various applications. In recent years, many algorithms have been proposed for solving SCP, especially local search algorithms have shown outstanding performance in solving ability. In this work, we develop an efficient local search algorithm named FastSC for SCP. First, we propose an improved configuration checking strategy to prevent the search from revisiting previously explored solutions. Second, we propose an adaptive subset selection strategy that dynamically adjusts the selection mode based on instance properties. Third, we implement a perturbation mechanism to help the algorithm escape local optima and explore promising solution spaces. Four, we present a new search mode that incorporates a gap line below the best-found solution to divide the search space into two parts and guide the algorithm toward a high-quality solution by adjusting the gap line. Experimental results show that FastSC is highly competitive with existing state-of-the-art algorithms, and particularly exhibits a distinct advantage on most challenging instances.

Title: Multi-agent collaborative reinforcement learning for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling under machine random failures
Authors: Haoze Wu, Vladimir Golovko, Marta Chodyka, Piotr Lichograj
Abstract: The dynamic flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP) demands improved scheduling efficiency, shortened production cycles, and balanced machining status of job shop machines. To address this, a dual-agent proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm integrating graph neural networks (GNN) and multi-head attention mechanisms, with the objectives of minimizing the maximum makespan, reducing machine idle rate, and enhancing machine load balancing rate is proposed. The DFJSP is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP) where the state space is constructed in the form of the heterogeneous graph. It defines the state and action spaces of the job and machine, designs a novel multi-objective reward function to minimize completion time, reduce machine idle rate, and improve machine load balancing rate, and establishes a dynamic hierarchical scheduling framework with two-stage collaborative processing of job selection and machine allocation. A novel multi-objective reward function is designed, and a dynamic hierarchical scheduling framework featuring two-stage collaborative processing—job selection and machine assignment—is established. The multi-head attention mechanism is introduced to strengthen the capability of capturing correlation features between job states and machine states, thereby improving the generalization performance of the policy and robustness against dynamic disturbances. Ablation experiments demonstrate that the proposed multi-head attention mechanism, dual-agent approach, and novel advantage estimation all improve the algorithm’s performance. Comparative experiments show that the proposed algorithm has significant advantages in terms of solution quality and generalization performance.

Title: Balancing power with logic: Exact satisfiability-based methods for energy-aware assembly lines
Authors: Zhifei Zheng, Sami Cherif, Matthieu Py, Rui S. Shibasaki, Chu-Min Li, Laurent Deroussi, Nathalie Grangeon
Abstract: The Simple Assembly Line Balancing Problem (SALBP) is a fundamental optimization challenge in the production and manufacturing domain. In this paper, we address a recently introduced variant, the Simple Assembly Line Balancing Problem with Power Peak Minimization (SALB3PM), which aims to minimize electricity consumption peaks. Despite the growing attention to this problem, existing approaches have yet to fully exploit the potential of logic-based methods. This work introduces exact solution approaches based on Satisfiability (SAT) and Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) formulations to tackle SALB3PM efficiently. A experimental study was carried out on a benchmark set of 300 instances derived from the literature, considering state-of-the-art solvers across multiple paradigms, including SAT, MaxSAT, Integer Linear Programming (ILP), Constraint Programming (CP) and Pseudo-Boolean Optimization (PBO). The results clearly show that the proposed satisfiability-based methods outperform integer linear formulations. In this sense, the strategies introduced in this paper offer promising perspectives for extension to other SALBP variants.

Title: A data envelopment analysis-informed neural network for production frontier estimation with soft regularization of production axioms
Authors: Xingyue Chen, Min Yang, Zixuan Wang, Liang Liang
Abstract: Estimating the production frontier is a fundamental task in technical efficiency analysis, with Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) being one of the most widely adopted methodologies. However, DEA often suffers from overfitting and limited generalizability due to its deterministic and non-statistical nature. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are a promising alternative for production frontier estimation, but most existing ANN-based models remain purely data-driven and lack theoretical grounding, leading to estimations that may be theoretically inconsistent or implausible. To address this limitation, we propose a novel model, named Data Envelopment Analysis-Informed Neural Network (DEAINN), which embeds the core assumptions of DEA, namely monotonicity, concavity, and the envelopment property, into the training process of the ANN through a soft regularization mechanism. Monte Carlo simulations show that DEAINN achieves competitive estimation error and favorable generalization performance relative to DEA, Corrected Concave Non-parametric Least Squares (C2[jls-end-space/]NLS), DEA-ANN, and Least-Squares Boosting (LSB)-Multivariate Adaptive Frontier Splines (MAFS) across diverse scenarios. In large-scale settings, DEAINN reduces computation time substantially relative to the benchmark methods as sample size increases. Finally, the proposed approach is applied to evaluate the energy utilization efficiency of 282 Chinese cities, with results demonstrating its practical applicability.

Title: Notification timing for on-demand personnel scheduling
Authors: Prakash Gawas, Antoine Legrain, Louis-Martin Rousseau
Abstract: We study the problem of dynamically timing shift notifications in on-demand staffing platforms, where experienced casual workers are prioritized through a priority ranking system. Workers are notified of available shifts in priority order, but delayed responses allow lower-priority workers to claim more desirable shifts, causing preference losses for higher-priority workers and undermining managerial efforts to retain a reliable workforce. Managers must also ensure that all available shifts are assigned within a limited planning horizon, despite uncertainty in worker response times. We formalize this trade-off as the Notification Timing Problem (NTP) and establish that even its simplified offline version is NP -complete. To address the dynamic stochastic problem, we propose two threshold-based heuristic policies—the Offline Notification Policy (ONP) and the Expected Buffer Policy (EBP)—derived from offline single-scenario solutions. Using real-world data from an industry partner managing over 15,000 workers across 1.4 million shifts annually, we demonstrate that the proposed policies significantly reduce preference losses and shift vacancies compared with the current notification strategy; in particular, ONP achieves up to a 10% improvement over the policy derived from the stochastic optimization model while reducing computation time from days to minutes.

Title: Editorial Board
Resource-constrained project scheduling for construction dust emission reduction
Authors: Yifei Li, Lihui Zhang, Zongyu Yao, Jinrong Zhu
Abstract: Construction dust is a primary source of urban particulate matter pollution, posing a significant threat to public health and the urban environment. Based on the fugitive emission characteristics of construction dust, this study proposes a novel control method. Unlike existing research that relies on changing activity execution modes to reduce environmental impact, the core of this method lies in leveraging dynamic variations of meteorological conditions to mitigate construction dust pollution solely by optimizing activity execution times. Building on this, the study introduces a novel Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem with Construction Dust Emission Reduction (RCPSP-CDER). By introducing a piecewise linear function to characterize the time-varying attributes of the meteorology-driven dust emission factor, a bi-objective optimization model for project duration and dust emissions is established. Two complementary solution approaches are developed: an ε[jls-end-space/]-constraint Constraint Programming exact method (ε C-CP) and an NSGA-II metaheuristic. The high-rise building case study reveals that significant reductions in construction dust emissions can be achieved through scheduling optimization, even under resource constraints and with no extension to project duration or increase in cost. Sensitivity analysis reveals the impact of meteorological conditions and resource capacity on the emission reduction potential. Computational experiments on PSPLIB benchmark instances across four scales show that ε C-CP attains solution quality comparable to NSGA-II on small-scale instances and recovers the exact Pareto front on a subset of them, thereby serving as a reliable benchmark; on medium- and large-scale instances, NSGA-II consistently outperforms ε C-CP in both Pareto front quality and computational efficiency. This study provides project managers with a robust quantitative decision-making tool to achieve dust reduction targets under practical engineering constraints.

Title: Revisiting local search for Curriculum-Based Course Timetabling
Authors: Sara Ceschia, Francesca Da Ros, Luca Di Gaspero, Andrea Schaerf
Abstract: Curriculum-Based Course Timetabling (CB-CTT) is a well-established benchmark problem in educational timetabling, with numerous real and synthetic datasets. Despite its long history of algorithmic developments, designing search methods that work effectively across diverse datasets under time limits remains challenging. In this paper, we focus on local search and, after a thorough analysis of all neighborhood structures reported in the literature, we propose an improved Simulated Annealing (SA) algorithm driven by an extended version of the classic LectureMove neighborhood, called LectureKick , that allows flexible lecture relocation while preserving feasibility. The neighborhood is further enriched with several sampling biases specifically designed to address the soft constraints of CB-CTT, while the overall behavior of the SA is regulated by a cut-off mechanism embedded in the cooling schedule. The method involves numerous parameters, both for the SA schedule and for the neighborhood biases, which are rigorously tuned on a large artificial dataset. The final algorithm is subsequently evaluated on the available benchmarks, including the “standard” ITC 2007 comp dataset, under the original competition timeout conditions. The results show that our approach clearly outperforms all previously proposed local search methods and is competitive with the best methods reported for CB-CTT overall, while improving upon them on several instances.

Title: Heuristics for the three-dimensional multiple bin size bin packing problem with transportation constraints
Authors: Sifan Cai, Zhenzhen Zhang, Ek Peng Chew, Kok Choon Tan, Haobin Li
Abstract: This paper studies a three-dimensional Multiple Bin Size Bin Packing Problem (3D-MBSBPP) with transportation constraints where the bins are Unit Load Devices (ULDs) designed specifically for fitting in aircraft. Specifically, the fragility, vertical stability, orientation and weight distribution of the boxes, as well as the specific shape and weight capacity of the ULDs, are taken into account. The target is to identify a packing plan with the minimum unused space to place the given set of rectangular boxes into various types of ULDs while satisfying the aforementioned constraints. To handle this complex problem, we develop a heuristic algorithm that first combines non-fragile boxes of the same height into blocks and packs them in the bottom of ULDs to provide more support space for other boxes. Then, for the remaining boxes, we extend the concept of residual space to ULDs to guide the placement, in which eight reference lines are designed to measure the relationship between the candidate box and the packed boxes. Moreover, to further reduce the unused space, we develop several movement strategies to intensively search for viable positions created by the possibly inclined wall of the ULDs and the top of non-adjacent non-fragile boxes. Additionally, we employ two strategies of moving all boxes and repacking some boxes to improve the weight distribution. The computational results show that our algorithm can achieve superior results in a short time on existing instances designed for this application and improves the best-known results in terms of filling rate and percentage of unbalanced ULDs. To better evaluate the proposed algorithm, we generate larger instances with more ULD types and various boxes. These instances and results can be used for future studies.

Title: Risk-averse antibiotics time machine problem
Authors: Deniz Tuncer, Burak Kocuk
Abstract: Antibiotic resistance, which is a serious healthcare issue, emerges due to uncontrolled and repeated antibiotic use that causes bacteria to mutate and develop resistance to antibiotics. The Antibiotics Time Machine Problem aims to come up with treatment plans that maximize the probability of reversing these mutations. Motivated by the severity of the problem, we develop a risk-averse approach and formulate a scenario-based mixed-integer linear program with a conditional value-at-risk objective function. We propose a risk-averse scenario batch decomposition algorithm that partitions the scenarios into manageable risk-averse subproblems, enabling the construction of lower and upper bounds. We develop several algorithmic enhancements in the form of stronger no-good cuts and symmetry breaking constraints in addition to scenario regrouping and warm starting. We conduct extensive computational experiments for static and dynamic versions of the problem on a real dataset and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our results suggest that risk-averse solutions can achieve significantly better worst-case performance compared to risk-neutral solutions with a slight decrease in terms of the average performance, especially for the dynamic version. Although our methodology is presented in the context of the Antibiotics Time Machine Problem, it can be adapted to other risk-averse problem settings in which the decision variables come from special ordered sets of type one.

Title: A new multiple-criteria group decision-making method within the robust ordinal regression framework
Authors: Jie Guo, Roman Słowiński, Zilong Wang, Zhiwen Zhang
Abstract: Real-world decision-making problems are often complex and multifaceted, requiring a group of decision-makers rather than a single individual, as well as a multiple-criteria evaluation of considered alternatives instead of the optimization of a single criterion. Because each decision-maker has a distinct knowledge background and value judgment, it is difficult to elicit consistent group preferences directly. A more realistic approach is to collect individual preference information and integrate it into a model that supports consensus-reaching around the best alternative. This study proposes a new multiple-criteria group decision-making method, grounded in the robust ordinal regression framework, which aligns with this approach. To reduce elicitation effort and cognitive burden, decision-makers provide preferences in the form of decision examples concerning reference alternatives that are relatively well known to them. Each example is assigned a confidence level (high, medium, or low), which is elicited from decision-makers and incorporated when constructing a value function compatible with the most reliable and consistent subset of the individual’s preferences. To address inconsistent preferences in the group, we introduce measures of support and opposition that help identify and adjust conflicting information. When decision-makers agree to revise their inputs to achieve consistency, the recommended alternative is identified through three complementary procedures: (i) a representative compatible value function, (ii) net flow scores from the necessary preference relation graph, and (iii) extreme ranking analysis. If consistency cannot be reached, the recommended alternative is determined by the rank-acceptability indices derived for individual decision-makers using stochastic multiobjective acceptability analysis. An illustrative case involving the multiple-criteria evaluation of teachers by a committee of experts demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed method.

Title: Operating room planning problem under uncertainty: A regret minimization model
Authors: Mohsen Roytvand Ghiasvand, Amin Ahmadi Digehsara, Amir Ardestani-Jaafari, Babak Mohamadpour Tosarkani, Pooya Pourrezaie-Khaligh
Abstract: Operating room (OR) planning presents a significant challenge for hospital managers due to inherent uncertainty in surgery durations, which are unknown at the time of scheduling. Decisions regarding the number of ORs to open and the assignment of surgeries must be made in advance, and inaccurate estimates can lead to idle capacity, excessive overtime, or delayed procedures. This study develops and compares three complementary optimization frameworks for OR planning under uncertainty: classical robust optimization (RO), regret minimization (RM), and a data-driven distributionally robust optimization (DRO) approach termed mean robust optimization (MRO). The RM model is designed to limit the maximum performance loss relative to an ex post optimal benchmark, thereby reducing excessive conservatism associated with worst-case planning. We show that both the RO and RM formulations admit equivalent robust counterparts and propose efficient column-and-constraint generation (C&CG) algorithms to solve large-scale instances. To leverage historical surgery duration data, we further incorporate the MRO framework, which constructs data-driven ambiguity sets through clustering and provides a tunable balance between robustness and data adaptivity. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate clear behavioral differences among the models. While RO yields the most conservative schedules, RM achieves lower worst-case costs at the expense of higher regret exposure under severe uncertainty, and MRO consistently delivers intermediate solutions that reduce conservatism while maintaining numerical stability. The results highlight how uncertainty severity, overtime cost structure, and data availability jointly influence model performance. From a managerial perspective, the proposed unified framework offers practical guidance for selecting OR planning models that align with institutional risk preferences and data maturity.

Title: Coordinating pilotage services across ports: A tri-objective optimization framework for cost, fairness, and safety
Authors: Baoli Liu, Yaomei Qiao, Dian Sheng, Jianfeng Zheng, Yuwei Xing
Abstract: Regional ports that are geographically adjacent or share overlapping pilotage waters can coordinate their pilotage operations to achieve more efficient and intensive use of resources. In this study, we consider the multi-port pilotage allocation and scheduling problem (MPPASP), in which a pilot dispatch center (PDC) manages a heterogeneous team of pilots, together with a fleet of pilot boats and helicopters, to provide pilotage services across a regional port cluster. The MPPASP is a generalization of the simultaneous pick-up and delivery vehicle routing problem with time windows, incorporating unique features such as diverse pilot requirements, multi-pilot synchronization, port-specific work regulations, and transport mode trade-offs. The objectives are to simultaneously minimize total operational costs, maximize service fairness across ports, and maximize pilotage safety. Despite its practical significance for regional port management, the MPPASP has not been well studied as reported in the literature. We formulate this new problem as a tri-objective mixed-integer program, based on which we develop a hybrid solution framework to solve it. The framework integrates evolutionary multi-objective search, guided by reinforcement learning for objective-oriented initialization and operator exploration, with optimization modules implemented via GUROBI to improve solution performance. Numerical experiments based on the field data from Beibu Gulf Port (comprising Qinzhou, Beihai, and Fangcheng Ports) in Guangxi, China, demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed solution framework compared to both the state-of-the-art solver and the benchmark algorithms from the literature. Sensitivity analyses provide managerial insights for PDCs, examining the optimal pilot grade composition together with the most suitable regional port cluster size and resource adjustments under seasonal demand fluctuations.

Title: Decision-aware robust Markov decision processes with distance-based uncertainty sets
Authors: Jun Zhou, Yisha Xiang, Ming Zhao
Abstract: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are widely used to model sequential decision-making under uncertainty, with applications such as maintenance optimization and inventory control. However, in many real-world settings, transition probabilities must be estimated from limited and noisy historical data, leading to significant estimation errors. Robust MDPs address this challenge by constructing ambiguity sets that, with high confidence, contain the true transition probabilities. While effective in guarding against worst-case scenarios, these models often produce overly conservative policies, especially when data are scarce. In this paper, we propose a novel decision-aware robust MDP framework that reduces conservatism by incorporating information from nominal policies and their performance. Specifically, we introduce a second ambiguity set centered at an alternative reference distribution, identified through an inverse MDP that enhances nominal performance. The intersection of this set with the conventional ambiguity set (centered at empirical distributions) forms a decision-aware uncertainty set. We provide tractable reformulations for ϕ[jls-end-space/]-divergence-based ambiguity sets and develop an efficient algorithm to seek robust yet less conservative policies. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the decision-aware approach achieves improved out-of-sample performance and yields worst-case distributions closer to the true distribution, highlighting its advantage over conventional robust MDPs.

Title: A double-stage heuristic algorithm for the antibandwidth maximization problem via the linear bottleneck assignment optimization
Authors: Jintong Ren, Jin-Kao Hao, Eduardo Rodriguez-Tello, Zequn Wei
Abstract: The antibandwidth maximization problem is a classic graph layout problem arising in applications such as multiprocessor scheduling, radio frequency assignment, and obnoxious facility location. It involves assigning distinct integer labels to the vertices of a graph such that the minimum absolute difference between the labels of adjacent vertices is maximized. To solve this NP-hard problem, we propose a double-stage heuristic algorithm integrating a local optimization stage with a dedicated reduced neighborhood, and a greedy optimized perturbation stage including a greedy assignment step as well as an optimized assignment step. Crucially, we demonstrate that the optimized assignment step can be transformed into solving the linear bottleneck assignment problem, which is solvable in polynomial time via a threshold algorithm. Experimental results across 256 benchmark instances show that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods by achieving 42 improved lower bounds while matching the best-known results on the majority of the remaining instances. Additional analysis confirms the critical contribution of the algorithm’s key components to its overall performance.

Title: A multi-objective dual hyper-heuristic approach for rescheduling in dynamic flexible job shop
Authors: Mengyuan Sun, Xi Zhang, Mingzhou Liu, Lin Ling, Maogen Ge, Jing Hu
Abstract: Predictive-reactive rescheduling combines pre-scheduling with real-time responses to maintain production stability under disturbances, and is extensively used in dynamic production environments. For multi-objective optimization of Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (DFJSP), the problem’s complexity increases significantly, challenging traditional algorithms to provide high-quality global solutions with low latency. This study proposes an innovative dual hyper-heuristic (DHH) method for rescheduling in DFJSP, aiming to generate rescheduling solutions in real-time and optimize two practical objectives: rescheduling stability and makespan. A rescheduling framework is proposed to decompose the global optimization problem into the sequence repair decision process based on the operation-to-interval transfer. The framework comprises two-stage hyper-heuristics: rule generation and selection. In the first stage, genetic programming is used to generate local repair heuristics as candidate action set. A double-tree encoding for selecting operations and intervals respectively is designed, and a terminal set combining real-time operating conditions and critical path characteristics is constructed to improve search efficiency. In the second stage, deep reinforcement learning is used to accurately relocate operations based on repair heuristics to achieve global optimization. A knowledge sharing pattern across scenarios is developed to enhance the generality of the algorithm. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark extensions demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms widely used multi-objective meta-heuristic algorithms while significantly reducing computation time.

Title: Improved variable neighborhood search for the min-degree constrained minimum spanning tree problem
Authors: Manisha Israni, Shyam Sundar
Abstract: The min-degree constrained minimum spanning tree (MDMST) problem is a well-known NP[jls-end-space/]-hard problem of finding a minimum-csot spanning tree while ensuring that every non-leaf vertex has degree at least d[jls-end-space/], where d is a constant positive integer. Degree constraints fundamentally reshape the feasible search space, often forcing the inclusion of longer edges to restore feasibility, which makes the problem particularly challenging. Based on these observations, this paper proposes an improved variable neighborhood search algorithm, denoted as (Formula presented), for the MDMST problem. Unlike the four existing VNS variants, which rely on random edge modifications, the proposed approach incorporates four structurally diverse, degree-based neighborhoods (N1 to N4[jls-end-space/]) that explicitly target edge modification associated with degree-critical vertices. These neighborhoods, combined with tailored local search strategies, enable more effective exploration and refinement of feasible solutions by balancing diversification and intensification in the search space. Extensive experimental analysis confirms the superiority of (Formula presented) over previous four variable neighborhood search variants. Its performance is also superior to state-of-the-art approaches particularly on instances of larger size. (Formula presented) discovers new best-known values on 43 out of 105 instances across all four data-sets, underscoring its capability to explore the search space effectively. Also, (Formula presented) requires only 2 tunable parameters, compared to 12 in the recent approach (Wu et al., 2025), highlighting its robustness and practical efficiency.

Title: Reinforcement learning-guided multi-objective particle swarm optimization with adaptive topology
Authors: Baotong Wu, Zhixiang Chen, Emrah Demir
Abstract: Multi-objective optimization problems often involve a trade-off between convergence toward the Pareto front and diversity along the front. This study proposes a reinforcement learning-guided multi-objective particle swarm optimization algorithm, called RL-MOPSO, which uses adaptive topology selection to manage this trade-off during the search. The algorithm combines three network topologies: global best, dual-population ring, and Von-Neumann topology with an adaptive jump collaboration operator. Q-learning selects among these topologies dynamically using feedback from convergence and distribution metrics. Computational experiments compare RL-MOPSO with 11 algorithms, including six state-of-the-art methods and five topology-based MOPSO variants. The results show that RL-MOPSO improves both convergence and diversity. The ablation experiments further confirm the contributions of Q-learning and the proposed topology structures.

Title: Conflict-aware seat assignment in classroom environments
Authors: Bruna Cristina Braga Charytitsch, Mariá Cristina Vasconcelos Nascimento
Abstract: Determining an effective seating plan is a key challenge in classroom management, as the spatial arrangement of students directly influences interpersonal dynamics and the overall learning environment. This paper introduces the Student Seat Allocation Problem (SSAP), which consists of strategically assigning students to seats in a traditional classroom, to minimize interpersonal conflicts while satisfying operational constraints. We propose a mathematical model and an Iterated Local Search (ILS) heuristic to address the SSAP. Computational experiments on a benchmark of 131 instances show that both methods converge to the optimal solution in 78 small- and medium-scale instances. For large-scale instances, Gurobi frequently exceeded the time limit, yet achieved very low optimality gaps, outperforming the heuristic’s average gap in 45 instances. ILS, in turn, outperformed Gurobi in 8 instances, and, when analyzing individual runs, successfully reached a gap of zero in multiple executions for several large-scale instances — within a fraction of Gurobi’s computational time. These results position ILS as an effective and accessible alternative for educational institutions where commercial solver licenses are unavailable or cost-prohibitive.

Title: Research on multi-resource flexible job shop scheduling considering flexible matching of pallets and workbenches
Authors: Zhifeng Liu, LinJing Wang, Jun Yan, Yueze Zhang, Yanhong Cheng, Qiang Cheng
Abstract: Pallets and workbenches are one of the main factors affecting production efficiency in multi resource flexible production during the preparation phase. The flexible matching of pallets and workbenches is key issue and directly affects production scheduling. For this purpose, a flexible job shop scheduling model is developed to address multi-stage operations involving setup, processing, and unloading, incorporating specific constraints on workbenches and pallets. An improved genetic algorithm for multi-stage resource-driven scheduling (IGA-MSRDS) is proposed, featuring three-layer encoding, dynamic optimization strategies, and resource-sensitive operators. The algorithm enhances task sequencing and resource coordination through cooperative crossover and load-aware mutation, and refines multi-resource handling via dynamic strategies. The experimental results of multiple benchmark instances demonstrate that IGA-MSRDS excels in scheduling performance. Especially in terms of solution quality and system adaptability under complex resource constraints.

Title: HELP-RL: Real-time policy optimization with hierarchical decoder for heterogeneous and stochastic disaster response logistics
Authors: Hadi Aghazadeh, Xin Wang
Abstract: Disaster response logistics plays a vital role in reducing existential risk in relief operations by ensuring that essential resources reach affected communities promptly during emergencies. Although its significance is widely recognized, existing studies tend to focus primarily on pre-disaster planning, leaving notable gaps in addressing the complex, dynamic, and unpredictable challenges of real-time disaster response. This paper introduces a new framework called HELP-RL ( Humanitarian Emergency Logistics Planning with Reinforcement Learning ) to address these challenges, which are grouped into three main categories: heterogeneous fleet types, diverse demand types, and stochastic travel times. Together, these reflect the real-world complexities of disaster response logistics, all of which require real-time management. The HELP-RL framework incorporates a unique hierarchical decoder to manage the intricate action space, paired with an efficiently designed attention-based policy optimizer using the REINFORCE algorithm. This fully integrated model is built to adapt dynamically to changing disaster conditions, providing reliable and real-time solutions. To assess its performance, we tested the framework using both synthetic and real-world data from wildfire response logistics, drawing on actual data to replicate realistic scenarios. The findings show that HELP-RL produces adaptable and optimal policies that effectively handle rapid changes, surpassing other reinforcement learning approaches in terms of both efficiency and practical applicability.

Title: On disperse generalized linear models
Authors: Emilio Carrizosa, Renato De Leone, Marica Magagnini
Abstract: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) are a key tool in Explainable Machine Learning, since they provide an easy-to-understand explanation of their coefficients and the impact of the different features in predictions. However, not all accurate GLMs may be equally appealing due to presence of secondary objectives such as sparsity or other measurement costs. For this reason, several methods have been proposed in the literature to address the multiobjective problem of joint optimization of accuracy and other secondary criteria, sparsity being the most popular objective if explainability is pursued. In this work we explore how different GLMs with good accuracy can be. We consider a biobjective P -Dispersion Problem, in which P models are sought jointly maximizing an overall accuracy measure as well as a dispersion measure. Several metrics are used to measure dispersion, such as a function of the distance between their parameters or the set of features used to predict. Moreover, different scenarios for the feasible region are considered, e.g., whether the P models are to be chosen from, or added to, a list of pre-selected GLMs. All these variants are expressed as biobjective nonlinear mixed integer optimization problems. Numerical tests are also presented, showing the effectiveness and the relevance of the proposed methodology.

Title: Instance scaling and metamodel-based sensitivity analysis for rolling horizon optimization with application to postal letter delivery services
Authors: Fabian Dunke, Stefan Nickel
Abstract: In many real-world planning settings, optimization problems are not only large in scale but also must be solved repeatedly as new data becomes available — most notably in rolling horizon schemes. However, this repeated solution process can quickly become computationally prohibitive, especially when assessing the sensitivity of outcomes to model parameters. We address this challenge by integrating two complementary methodological components: First, we propose an instance scaling technique using approximate linear scaling, which systematically reduces problem size to ensure computational tractability with limited loss of solution fidelity. Second, we develop a metamodel-based sensitivity analysis that efficiently displays the relationship between model parameters and solution process outcomes. Using surrogate models such as regression and neural networks, this approach enables fast estimation of both local and global sensitivities, even in complex sequential optimization processes where direct evaluation would require excessive computational effort. Together, these methodological advances form the foundation of a framework for efficiently analyzing the input–output relationships of optimization models used in rolling-horizon schemes. From a practical perspective, the framework enables informed decision-making through systematic alignment of strategic parameter setting in accordance with operational performance. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated for the postal letter delivery services, where it is used to examine the influence of different strategic measures, such as requiring specific delivery service levels or (dis-)incentivizing postponed and express deliveries, upon actual postal operations.

Title: A dual GCN–MCTS framework for yield-aware scheduling in multistage manufacturing
Authors: Sugyeong Lee, Dong-Hee Lee
Abstract: Yield in semiconductor manufacturing is strongly path-dependent, as lots processed through different machine sequences can achieve substantially different final yields even under comparable throughput conditions. Yet conventional scheduling research has focused almost exclusively on productivity metrics, leaving quality-aware scheduling largely unexplored. This paper proposes a dual Graph Convolutional Network (GCN)-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework for yield-aware scheduling in a multistage manufacturing process with parallel machines, where the objective is to maximize product yield while preserving production throughput. The framework integrates two complementary GCN components—a Regression GCN (RegGCN) that learns a path-to-yield value function from historical path-yield records, and a Policy GCN (PolGCN), trained through offline policy distillation from RegGCN, that provides state-conditioned action priors over feasible machine assignments for MCTS under real-time machine availability. These components are integrated into a Progressive Value Integration PUCT (PVI-PUCT) selection mechanism that adaptively blends RegGCN value estimates with simulation statistics as tree search matures, enabling informed decisions from the earliest search iterations. Experiments are conducted on a simulated semiconductor dataset incorporating machine-level main effects and adjacent-stage interaction effects that preclude purely additive yield prediction. Results show that RegGCN achieves an R2 of 0.9984 using only 5% of all feasible paths, and that the proposed framework improves yield by +11.18 percentage points over a random baseline while maintaining comparable throughput, matching the performance of parameter-tuned heuristics without requiring sensitivity analysis or parameter selection. The analysis further reveals that the GCN value function provides the primary yield-improvement signal, while MCTS lookahead prevents throughput degradation by accounting for future machine availability in early dispatching decisions. These results demonstrate that process-path data can be transformed into actionable scheduling decisions for yield improvement without requiring additional sensors or inline inspection data.

Title: A batch approximate evaluation method for neighborhood solutions in job shop scheduling
Authors: Zhiyong Ba, Jinduo Liu, Yiping Yuan
Abstract: Efficient neighborhood evaluation is critical for local search in the Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSP). To address the high evaluation cost and strong computational redundancy in neighborhood evaluation, this paper focuses on the well-known N7 neighborhood and proposes a slack-time–based batch approximate evaluation method. The method constructs a slack-time recursion model to enable independent updates of operation head and tail lengths during evaluation. Based on domain knowledge of different N7 move types, a structured batch evaluation framework is further developed, reducing the complexity of batch approximate evaluation to linear time. Computational results show that the proposed method maintains high accuracy, achieves substantial speedups over classical and improved Balas-based evaluations as well as low-thread parallel Balas implementations, and improves the search performance of tabu search.

Title: Budget allocation via data-driven distributionally robust probability maximization
Authors: Belleh Fontem
Abstract: This paper studies a data-driven distributionally robust probability maximization problem arising in risk-averse budget allocation with binary random outcomes and concave response functions. The decision-maker seeks to allocate a limited budget across multiple endeavors to maximize the worst-case probability that the aggregate return exceeds a prescribed threshold. Because the underlying joint success probabilities are unknown, we construct an ambiguity set around the empirical distribution using a total-variation radius calibrated to achieve a certain finite-sample guarantee.
